conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived. We’ll be using a short screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a well-studied set of ten questions that helps us spot signs of depression, anxiety, and—most important—anything that might indicate you’re feeling unsafe or overwhelmed.  

Everything we talk about stays between us unless there’s an immediate safety concern, and my goal is simply to understand how you’ve been doing this past week. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to hear your honest experience so we can connect you with the right support.  

I’ll read each question once, and you can answer however feels most comfortable. Ready to start?  

Here’s the first one:  
Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?
Honestly… most of the time it feels kind of hard. My sister sent me a silly meme yesterday and I half-smiled, but I didn’t really laugh. Nothing seems that funny lately—I’m too tired, I guess.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I wouldn’t go that far. I can still chuckle once in a while—like when the baby makes those funny milk-drunk faces—but it’s not the easy, belly-laugh feeling I used to have. Most of the time it feels forced or just doesn’t happen at all.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I keep telling myself I should be excited about little outings—like when my mom offers to drive me to the farmers’ market—but when the time comes I just feel… flat. Even coffee with a friend feels like another chore to get through.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a couple of times this week. Yesterday the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe my milk isn’t good enough or I’m doing something wrong. I know rationally it’s probably just a growth-spurt thing, but the thought still pops in that I should be handling it better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Kind of. I’ll be sitting there feeding her and suddenly my heart races thinking, “What if she spits up and chokes when I’m not looking?” Nothing’s actually happening, but the worry sticks anyway. It’s not every hour, but most days it shows up at least once.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times, yeah. Like last night when she was sleeping longer than usual—instead of feeling relieved, my chest got tight and I kept imagining something awful had happened. I knew it was irrational, but I still crept in to check her breathing twice.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days they do. Between feeding every couple hours, trying to nap when she naps (which rarely works), and the mound of laundry that never shrinks, I feel like I’m always one step behind. Some mornings I wake up already tired and think, “How am I going to get through today?”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly “so unhappy,” but I do lie there running through everything I might have messed up—did I burp her long enough, is that rash normal, will I ever feel like myself again? It takes me a while to drift off, and when she squeaks I’m instantly awake. Several nights this week it’s happened.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I do feel sad some of the time. It’s not every minute, but little moments hit me—like when I see pictures of myself smiling before she was born and I think, “Who is that person?” I end up tearing up, then feeling silly for crying.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not that bad. I’ve teared up a couple of times, but I haven’t had those can’t-stop sobbing spells. It’s more like my eyes sting, I wipe them, and try to move on.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt tired and overwhelmed, but I haven’t had any thoughts of hurting myself.

It sounds like the past week has felt heavy-laughing rarely comes easily, activities that used to excite you now feel flat, and waves of worry or sadness catch you off-guard. You're working so hard to care for your baby while running on empty, and it's understandable that the constant demands leave you wondering how you'll get through the day.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, mild chuckles and notes most laughter feels absent or forced, aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-complete loss of anticipatory pleasure (anhedonia), describing activities as feeling 'flat' and like a 'chore,' aligning with 'Hardly at all.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a couple of times this week" and gives a specific example, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring, intrusive worries that arise without real danger and persist "most days at least once," aligning with "Yes, sometimes."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports discrete episodes of panic (tight chest, intrusive thoughts) without clear trigger, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to manage daily tasks, and waking already exhausted—matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient denies feeling "so unhappy" but describes persistent nighttime rumination and interrupted sleep most nights this week, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges frequent sadness triggered by memories, indicating "quite often" level</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map to core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: anhedonia (Q1, Q2 scored 2 and 3), <sym>depressed mood</sym> (Q8 score 2), <sym>guilt</sym> (Q3 score 2), <sym>anxiety</sym> (Q4, Q5 scored 2 each), feeling overwhelmed (Q6 score 3), and sleep disturbance (Q7 score 2). Total 19 exceeds the 14-point cut-off indicating high probability of depression. No self-harm ideation (Q10 score 0) is reassuring but does not negate clinical concern. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>primary care physician</med> to review results and consider therapy or medication options
2. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor symptom trajectory
3. Begin evidence-based counselling such as <med>interpersonal therapy</med> or <med>CBT</med> focused on postpartum issues
4. Share these results with a trusted support person who can accompany you to appointments
5. Practice 15-20 minutes of gentle outdoor walking daily and accept help with household tasks to reduce overload
6. Maintain sleep-hygiene routine: dim lights for night feeds, limit screen time before bed, and nap when baby naps if possible
7. Contact local <med>postpartum support group</med> or national helpline for peer support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
